newsitem.title: CANADA: Fletcher Canada to focus on paper growth.
newsitem.headline: Fletcher Canada to focus on paper growth.

text.p: Fresh from divesting its stake in TimberWest Forest Ltd, Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd pledged Wednesday to focus on expanding its paper business and did not rule out further talks with MacMillan Bloedel Ltd over its paper division.

Fletcher Canada, which is majority owned by New Zealand's Fletcher Challenge Ltd, said it will receive C$348 million for its 53 percent of TimberWest. The lumber company will also refinance C$240 million in debt owed to Fletcher.
TimberWest shareholders on Wednesday approved the sale of the company to a group of institutional investors who are turning it into an income trust.
Fletcher Canada spurred the sale process, saying TimberWest did not fit with its focus on paper.
Fletcher president Doug Whitehead said Wednesday his company wanted to "narrow our focus...and grow in pulp and more particularly in our printing papers business."
The industry's current landscape has lead Fletcher to conclude that "acquisition rather than building new (plants) is the right way to go," Whitehead said.
There has been persistent speculation that MacMillan Bloedel wants to sell its ailing paper operations and that Fletcher would be the most likely buyer.

MacMillan chief Robert Findlay said last month that a merger of the unit with another paper maker was the logical step but that years of talks with Fletcher Canada had failed to bear fruit. Findlay said he doubted the two companies would ever agree to a deal because of divergent goals.
Whitehead was more ambiguous Wednesday, telling reporters that nothing had been ruled out.
"The discussions (with MacMillan) are dormant," he said. "...(But) they could come back on. It's not a linear process."
He said that Findlay's comments may have been accurate at the time but they "may not be correct today."
When pressed to clarify what this meant, Whitehead said he was merely trying to emphasize that "circumstances change" and that shareholders of either company could mandate a change in course.
The industry needs to consolidate and there are discussions underway among many players, he added.
